title: MuddyWater
summary: MuddyWater is a widely tracked espionage activity set that public reporting has connected to Iranian state interests with moderate confidence, and vendors have labelled it Seedworm, Static Kitten and Mango Sandstorm among other names. It has been reported since around 2017, which makes it one of the most consistently documented Iranian linked intrusion sets. Typical victims are government bodies, telecommunications providers, oil and gas companies and universities, mainly in the Middle East, with occasional targeting elsewhere. The tradecraft is opportunistic rather than elegant: spear phishing with documents and links, abuse of legitimate remote monitoring and management software, renamed copies of system utilities, PowerShell based remote access tooling, and exploitation of unpatched public facing applications such as virtual private network and email gateways. Public reporting has repeatedly noted that the group reuses publicly available tools and occasionally leaks its own tooling, which complicates attribution and creates overlaps with ordinary criminal activity. Evidence in an environment includes suspicious document lures, PowerShell processes with encoded arguments, remote administration tools installed outside the normal change process, cloud storage endpoints in network logs, and bulk access to mailboxes or shared drives. Defenders should not dismiss the activity as commodity noise simply because the tooling is noisy; the intent is still long term intelligence collection, and the same access can be sold or reused by other actors.

beginner.definition: MuddyWater is a name security companies use for a spying group that public reports link to Iranian state interests. That link is an assessment, not a proven fact. The group has targeted governments and telephone companies since around 2017. It often uses ordinary tools instead of rare, custom malware.
beginner.whyItMatters: Because the group uses common tools and common cloud services, its traffic can look like normal work. A single alert may seem unimportant. Attackers like this also enter through unpatched remote access services. If you ignore small alerts, a slow spying campaign can continue for months.
howItWorks: The attacker sends targeted emails with a document, a link or a fake login page.
Some campaigns break into remote access services that were never updated or patched.
Once inside, the attacker runs built-in system tools to explore the network quietly.
Legitimate remote management software is installed and then used as a backdoor.
Data is copied from mailboxes and file shares and sent to cloud storage services.
The attacker keeps access by adding accounts, keys or scheduled tasks that survive reboots.
beginner.example: Imagine a repair company that fixes office air conditioning. The engineers wear the building uniform, carry the correct toolbox, and sign the visitor book. Nobody stops them, because everything about them looks normal. An intruder who buys the same uniform and copies the toolbox can move through the building all day. MuddyWater works the same way. It borrows real administrative tools, real cloud services and real company procedures. The disguise is made from your own environment.
takeaways: Watch for administrative tools used at strange times, from strange places, by the wrong accounts.
Patch internet facing services quickly, because they are a common way in for this group.
Turn on multi factor authentication for email, remote access and cloud accounts.

objectives: Explain how abuse of legitimate remote management software can hide an intrusion.
Recognise suspicious PowerShell execution and encoded command arguments in endpoint telemetry.
Describe how unpatched internet facing services become an entry point.
List the identity controls that reduce the impact of a successful phishing campaign.
Explain where public attribution for this group is strong and where it remains an assessment.
